pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 6–8 years

- **Topic:** Light & Seeing in the Dark

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 3 Science, Light):** recognise that they need light in order to see things and that dark is the absence of light.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 1-PS4-2):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]. (No assessment boundary; the clarification allows illumination from an external source OR from an object giving off its own light.)

- **Operational details:** Teach this as a felt, hands-on contrast rather than a told fact. The canonical activity is a dark den / blackout tent (Oak lists blindfolds and opaque materials as the equipment) in which children discover they cannot see, then introduce a small light and watch objects reappear. Elicit-predict-observe: ask what they will see before the light goes out. Establish the precise vocabulary — *dark means "without light"* — and separate two ideas that children blur: a lamp or screen is a light SOURCE (visible in the dark because it makes its own light) whereas a toy is a non-source (visible only when light reaches it). Reinforce that when there is no light we rely on other senses (touch, hearing). Note that true darkness is genuinely hard to achieve in a classroom, so plan the den carefully and run a risk assessment.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). At 6–8 this is a concrete, sensory achievement: the child observes that removing light removes sight and articulates that dark is the absence of light, not a substance. The threshold is overturning the intuition that we can see in the dark once our eyes "get used to it" — gains come from direct experience of true darkness, not from explanation. Mastery here is observational (we need light to see) and does not yet require the source→object→eye light-path model, which is built later in "How We See Objects."
bestPractices: Run a hands-on dark-den / blackout-tent experience so children directly feel that no light means no sight, then reintroduce a small light and watch objects reappear — the felt contrast does the teaching, not the telling.
Use an elicit–predict–observe cycle: ask children to predict what they will see as the light is removed, then check.
Explicitly distinguish light SOURCES (visible in the dark because they make their own light) from non-sources (visible only when light reaches them) with a sort of luminous vs non-luminous objects.
Teach and rehearse precise language: 'dark means without light'; contrast 'a little light' (can just see) with 'no light' (cannot see at all).
Discuss reliance on other senses (hearing, touch) when there is no light, to make the absence of sight concrete.
Plan for the difficulty of achieving true darkness and carry out a risk assessment for the den/blindfold activity (adult supervision).
keyRepresentations: Dark den / blackout tent or sensory room — the room itself as the manipulable variable (light in vs light out)
A torch plus a set of everyday objects, revealed and hidden by turning the light on and off
A luminous-vs-non-luminous sorting set (lamp, screen, glow-stick vs toy, book, spoon)
Simple before/after scene: the same objects shown lit and unlit
commonMisconceptions: Humans can see in the dark once their eyes adjust (the central Oak-flagged misconception: people can see with a little light but not with none).
Darkness is a thing in its own right — 'blackness' is a kind of light or substance — rather than simply the absence of light.
All objects we can see make their own light (failing to separate sources from reflectors).
Only hot or bright objects give out light.
Eyes can 'reach out' and see objects without light (an early form of the extramission idea built on later).

learn.summary: For children aged 6–8: they need light in order to see, and dark is the absence of light (not a substance). The threshold insight is overturning the intuition that we can see in the dark once our eyes 'get used to it' — for this specific misconception the shift comes most directly from experiencing true darkness, not from being told. A hands-on dark-den/blackout experience (predict → observe → explain) carries the core teaching; a dimmable scene lets the disappearance be run repeatedly on demand; sorting luminous vs non-luminous objects then serves as an end-check that assesses the conclusion. Mastery here is observational (we need light to see); the full source→object→eye light-path model is built later.

activities.title: Dark den: does the light leave, or the dark arrive?
feedback: If a child predicts the toys will appear after waiting, revisit together: in a truly light-tight space there is no light at all, so there is nothing to see however long you wait — hunt for where any 'little bit of light' might sneak in in a normal bedroom.
If a child talks about the dark 'covering' or 'coming in' over the toys, reframe: you add light to see; you don't scoop out or remove dark. Darkness is the absence of light.
When the torch reveals only objects in its beam, point out that light must actually reach an object for us to see it.
activities.rationale: The target misconception (seeing in the dark after eyes adjust) is best challenged by felt experience of true darkness rather than telling. The elicit–predict–observe cycle surfaces the child's intuition before the contrast overturns it. True darkness is genuinely hard to achieve in a classroom, so the den needs careful planning and a risk assessment.
sourceClaims: Year 3 'Light and seeing' learning points: we need light to see; darkness is when there is no light; 'dark means without light'; common misconception explicitly named is 'humans can see without light' (can see with a little light but not none); equipment is blindfolds and opaque materials for dark dens.
NGSS 1-PS4-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]' — illumination can be external or from an object giving off its own light; no assessment boundary listed.

Canonical light misconceptions to anticipate include 'we can see in the dark' and 'blackness is a form of light rather than an absence of light'; darkness is the absence of light and we cannot see in true darkness.
learnerActions: Before the light goes out, predict aloud what you will see: will the objects slowly appear if you wait, or vanish? Say why first.
Sit in a carefully planned, as-dark-as-possible den/blackout tent with everyday objects — a teddy, a book, a cup — and a small torch or lamp nearby, under adult supervision.

With the light off, notice whether you can see the objects. If the den is truly dark you cannot see them at all; if you can see them faintly, hunt for where a little light is getting in. Name what else you can tell using touch and hearing.
Turn on a small light and watch the objects reappear; describe what actually happened versus your prediction.
Sweep a torch beam around and report which objects become visible — mainly the ones the beam reaches (light bouncing off nearby walls may light others faintly).
activities.intendedInsight: We can only see objects when light reaches them and our eyes; in genuine darkness there is nothing to see no matter how long we wait. The teddy did not leave — the light did. Dark is light that is absent, not a thing that arrived.

activities.title: Dimmable scene: run the disappearance yourself
feedback: If a child expects an unlit toy to stay visible, point to the fading: the toy is still in the room, but with no light reaching it there is nothing to see.
If a child is surprised the lamp still shows in the dark, highlight that it makes its own light, so it does not need light from elsewhere.
Reinforce that only the objects inside the torch cone reappear — light has to reach them.
activities.rationale: A brightness control simulates the dark-den moment on demand and lets a child repeat a model of the experience, which is hard to do safely and repeatedly with a real blacked-out room. The live recolouring/fading of objects and the movable torch cone show the 'light must reach it' idea. This is a scaffold for, not a replacement of, felt darkness.
sourceClaims: Year 3 'Light and seeing' learning points: we need light to see; darkness is when there is no light; 'dark means without light'; common misconception explicitly named is 'humans can see without light' (can see with a little light but not none); equipment is blindfolds and opaque materials for dark dens.
NGSS 1-PS4-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]' — illumination can be external or from an object giving off its own light; no assessment boundary listed.
learnerActions: Look at a cosy bedroom scene with a brightness control (a slider or a light-switch, optionally with a torch).
Predict what will happen to each object as you lower the light, then slowly drag the brightness down to zero.
Notice which things fade and vanish (the teddy, book, cup) and which one still glows in the dark (a switched-on screen or night-light that stays on) because it makes its own light.
Flick on the torch and sweep its cone around; report that only objects the beam reaches pop back into view while everything outside the cone stays invisible.
Run the dimming several times to confirm the same thing happens each time.
activities.intendedInsight: Lowering the light makes non-luminous objects disappear even though they are still there, while a light source stays visible in the dark. Light must reach an object for it to be seen.

activities.title: Sort: makes its own light vs needs light to be seen
feedback: If a child calls a mirror or a white wall a light source, do the lights-off test; for the Moon, which can't be tested in class, discuss where its light really comes from (the Sun).
If a child sorts correctly, ask them to justify one case aloud to check the reasoning, not just the answer.
Watch for 'only hot or bright things give light' — include a cool glow-stick or screen as a source to broaden the idea.
activities.rationale: Children blur light sources and reflectors; an explicit sort with the torch-on/off test and the Moon as a key case targets that confusion. A sort like this can teach and check classification but does not itself produce the first-hand observation that earns the insight, so it works best after the den/dimmer experience.
sourceClaims: NGSS 1-PS4-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]' — illumination can be external or from an object giving off its own light; no assessment boundary listed.
learnerActions: Take a mixed set of objects — lamp, screen, glow-stick, torch (sources); teddy, book, spoon, a mirror, the Moon (non-sources/reflectors).
Sort each into 'makes its own light' or 'only seen when light reaches it'.
Use a lights-off test: in a dark space, which objects still show (switched-on or glowing sources) and which disappear? Remember a lamp, torch or screen makes light only while it is switched on.
Decide where the Moon goes and explain: it is visible because it bounces light from the Sun, so it does not make its own light.
Say in your own words what you need in order to see any of the objects that do not make their own light.
activities.intendedInsight: Some objects give off their own light (sources); most objects we see only reflect light that reaches them. Being bright or shiny does not make something a light source.

activities.title: Talk-it-through: scooping out the dark
feedback: If the child says the dark can be scooped out, steer to: the way to make dark go away is to add light, so dark is the absence of light.

If they say they can adapt to total darkness, separate a sealed dark room from a dim room where light leaks in — eyes can get more sensitive, but with genuinely zero light there is still nothing to see.
Praise reasoning that appeals to the total absence of light rather than to eyes adjusting.
activities.rationale: Short, responsive discussion lets children rehearse and defend the 'absence of light' idea and tackle the darkness-as-substance and dark-adaptation errors in words, supporting the precise vocabulary 'dark means without light'. Talk can rehearse and check the explanation but does not itself produce the felt experience that carries the core insight, so it supplements the den/dimmer rather than replacing them.
sourceClaims: Canonical light misconceptions to anticipate include 'we can see in the dark' and 'blackness is a form of light rather than an absence of light'; darkness is the absence of light and we cannot see in true darkness.

Year 3 'Light and seeing' learning points: we need light to see; darkness is when there is no light; 'dark means without light'; common misconception explicitly named is 'humans can see without light' (can see with a little light but not none); equipment is blindfolds and opaque materials for dark dens.
learnerActions: Discuss: 'If darkness were really a thing, could you scoop it out of the room with a cup? So what actually makes the dark go away?'
Answer whether the Moon is a light source or only bounces light from somewhere else.
A friend says 'I can see a bit in my bedroom at night.' Work out where that little bit of light might be sneaking in from.
State in your own words why a truly light-tight room stays invisible no matter how long you wait.
activities.intendedInsight: You add light to make the dark go away; you do not remove a substance. Eyes really do become more sensitive after a while, so in a real bedroom where a little light gets in you can see more over time; but true darkness leaves nothing to see.

constraints: Target age is 6–8; mastery here is observational (we need light to see) and does not yet require the source→object→eye light-path model, which is built later in work on how we see objects.
True darkness is genuinely hard to achieve in a classroom: plan the den/blindfold activity carefully and carry out a risk assessment with adult supervision.
Teach the precise vocabulary: 'dark means without light'; contrast 'a little light' (can just see) with 'no light' (cannot see at all).

A dimmable on-screen scene is a scaffold that lets the disappearance be repeated on demand; it asserts and demonstrates the idea, while the felt experience of real darkness is what most directly overturns the intuition for this misconception. Use both where possible.
Sorting and end-check questions assess the conclusion; a sort can teach/check classification but does not itself produce the first-hand observation, so schedule it after the hands-on experience.
Reinforce reliance on other senses (touch, hearing) when there is no light, to make the absence of sight concrete.

A narrated character or cave explorer can add atmosphere but tends to tell the answer rather than let the child observe; the core insight here is in the felt darkness, so do not let narration replace the observation.
Include cool light sources (glow-stick, screen) when sorting, so children do not conclude only hot or bright objects give out light.

Scoped alternative — a static lit/unlit scene with tap-to-reveal labels can name sources vs reflectors, but it asserts the idea rather than letting the child run the objects' disappearance as the light leaves; prefer the dimmable scene or felt den where the child controls the change.

Scoped alternative — a walk-through 3D dark room can add immersion/atmosphere, but 'we need light to see' is not a spatial concept, so it may add cost without clearly sharpening the insight that the 2D dimmer and the felt den already deliver.
The extramission idea ('eyes reach out to see') is deferred to later work; it is noted here only so it is not reinforced, and is not a target for this concept.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated a static lit/unlit image as only 'possible' ('a static picture cannot deliver' the felt disappearance), rated 3D as adding 'cost without sharpening the insight', and a conversation as 'poor' because it would 'just tell the child the answer'. These were catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; they have been softened to scoped trade-offs (static images assert rather than let a child run the change; 3D adds immersion but not spatial insight; narration risks telling the answer) and the static/3D alternatives are now stated as scoped-alternative constraints rather than dropped.
The original claim that a live dimmer is 'exactly the repeated direct experience the misconception needs' overstates equivalence with real darkness; retained as a scaffold with its limit stated.
One source (IOP light resource) was marked verified:false in the row; treat its misconception claims as un-reverified.

The Moon example as a reflector is pedagogically standard and consistent with the source note on objects that give off their own light vs reflect it; included in sorting and discussion as the key transfer case.

No source[].claim directly states 'sort sources from reflectors'; the source/reflector sorting rationale is supported only by the NGSS wording about illumination 'from an object giving off its own light', so the Oak claim has been removed from that activity's sourceClaims as topical rather than directly supporting.

The row's extramission misconception ('eyes can reach out and see without light') is flagged in the row as an idea built on later; it is deferred here rather than taught, and recorded in the preservation audit so it is not silently lost.

assess.poeTask: Predict what you will see when we shut you inside the light-tight box (or put on the blackout blindfold) and wait two minutes — will the objects slowly appear? Say why first. Then try it and explain what actually happened.
probeDeeper: Is the Moon a light source, or does it only bounce light that comes from somewhere else?
Your friend says 'I can see a bit in my bedroom at night.' Where might that little bit of light be sneaking in from?
If darkness were really a thing, could you scoop it out of the room with a cup? So what actually makes the dark go away?
assess.correctAnswer: No. In complete darkness there is no light at all, so there is nothing to see no matter how long you wait. You can only see when some light reaches the objects and your eyes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Dark adaptation: 'if I wait, my eyes get used to the dark and then I can see' — the tell is 'at night I can see my room after a while'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish a truly sealed dark room from a dim room where light leaks in; do the light-tight-box or blindfold experience — you never adapt to genuinely zero light. Hunt for where the 'little bit of light' was sneaking in before.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — if you wait, your eyes get used to the dark and you can see the toys.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says yes, the toys will become visible after waiting; appeals to eyes adjusting

errorPatterns.pattern: Darkness as a substance: 'the dark is a thing that fills the room and covers the toys' (like fog or a blanket)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe dark as the ABSENCE of light, not a substance; watch the 'light chases the dark away' language, which reinforces darkness-as-stuff. You add light; you don't remove dark.
errorPatterns.distractor: You can't see because the darkness is covering the toys.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about dark 'coming in' or 'covering' things as if it were a material you could remove

errorPatterns.pattern: Source/reflector confusion: anything bright is a 'light source' — the Moon, a mirror, a white wall all 'make light'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort objects into makes-its-own-light versus only-reflects-light; the torch-on-versus-off test and the Moon (bounces the Sun's light) are the key cases.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the Moon or a shiny/bright object a light source

responseLevels.gap: Says you can see in total darkness once your eyes adjust, or treats darkness as a substance that covers the toys.
responseLevels.full: States you can see ONLY when light reaches the objects and your eyes; explains that a truly light-tight room stays invisible forever; and correctly sorts sources (make their own light) from reflectors (bounce light), transferring to the Moon.
responseLevels.partial: Knows you need light to see, but still thinks a genuinely sealed dark room would become visible with enough time, OR cannot reliably tell light sources from objects that only reflect light.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Imagine a room with NO light at all — every window sealed, every crack blocked, completely dark. You sit inside for a long, long time. Can you see the toys in the room if you just wait long enough for your eyes to get used to the dark? Tell me what you think and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Every 'dark' bedroom a child has known actually has a little light leaking in, which teaches 'eyes get used to it'. The prompt specifies ZERO light, so the child who over-generalises dark-adaptation says yes (wrong), while the child who grasps 'no light means nothing to see' says no. The reason they give — whether they appeal to eyes adjusting or to the total absence of light — is the tell.
